666.title: Rejoice always (Philippians 4:4–7)
666.hook: the Lord is near; don't be anxious; the peace that passes understanding
666.howItsDone: Philippians 4:4–7 is read in many churches during Advent, and the words about the peace of God are used as a blessing at the end of services in several traditions, including Anglican worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Euodia and Syntyche, asked to agree, and your line was be of one mind.

Three in the morning. The ceiling. The list running in your head: the bill, the test result, the thing you said, the thing you didn't say. Worry is very good at its job. It feels like doing something, and it does nothing. Now consider where these next lines were written. Not from a beach. Paul is in custody, waiting to learn whether he'll live or die. And the next thing he writes is a command to be glad. Not once. Twice.

In the King James Bible: "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice." Note the small words: in the Lord. Paul isn't telling anyone to feel happy about everything that happens. He's pointing at where the joy is anchored. Then: "Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand." Moderation here is gentleness, a kind of give, the opposite of insisting on your rights. And the Lord is at hand can be heard two ways, and both may be meant: he is coming soon, and he is close by right now. Then worry. The King James says: "Be careful for nothing." In the King James's English, careful meant full of care, anxious. Don't be anxious about anything. And instead, a practice: "but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God." Every thing, small things too. And notice with thanksgiving tucked in the middle, like a stone in a shoe. You bring the worry, and a thank-you alongside it. Then the promise: "And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus." The word for keep is a military word. It means to guard, the way soldiers garrison a town. Peace stands at the gate of the heart. Not a peace that makes sense of everything. A peace that goes past understanding, and holds anyway.
screen: `IN THE LORD: JOY WITH AN ANCHOR.`

segments.voice: Name one worry, the one most likely to wake you tonight, plainly and whole. Then, right beside it, name one thing you're thankful for; it doesn't need to fix the worry, just sit next to it. If you pray, make both known to God in your own words, as Paul says; if you don't, simply let the two sit together while you breathe.
Rejoice always. Paul's double command from prison: rejoice in the Lord, again rejoice, and bring every worry with thanksgiving.
Your line: the peace that passes understanding. A guard at the gate of the heart. See you tomorrow.

667.title: Whatever is lovely (Philippians 4:8–9)
667.hook: whatever is true, noble, pure, lovely: think on these things
667.howItsDone: Some Christians use Philippians 4:8 as a test for what they read, watch and talk about.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a peace that stands guard at the heart, and your line was the peace that passes understanding.

An argument between strangers. A crime two states away. Someone's perfect kitchen. An ad that knew what you'd been thinking about. Ten minutes on a phone, and all of that went in. None of it was chosen, exactly. It just arrived, and it stayed. Paul has just promised the Philippians a peace that will guard their hearts and minds. Now he tells them what to let through the gate. He gives them a list.

Here it is in the King James Bible, worth hearing slowly: "Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things." Six whatsoevers, then two ifs. Honest, in the old English, means honorable, worthy of respect. Of good report: things that speak well. The word for lovely is an unusual one. It means pleasing, winsome, the kind of thing that makes you want to come closer. And a surprise: some of these words, virtue especially, were also at home among the Greek moral philosophers. Paul borrows the vocabulary that thoughtful people in a Greek city already used about the good life. He seems to say: whatever is genuinely good, wherever you find it, take it in. Then the verb: think on these things. The Greek means to reckon, to count up, to dwell on deliberately, the same verb Paul used when he said he didn't count himself to have arrived. This isn't wishful thinking or ignoring what's wrong. It's choosing what you keep turning over. And he doesn't leave it as thinking: "Those things, which ye have both learned, and received, and heard, and seen in me, do: and the God of peace shall be with you." Think on them, then do them. Yesterday, the peace of God. Today, the God of peace.

Pick one thing from the last few days that was true, or good, or simply lovely: a child's laugh, light on a wall, someone keeping a promise, a song. Stay with it on purpose, the place, the sound, the color, and when your mind drifts back to a worry, bring it gently back to the lovely thing. If you pray, you can give thanks for it.
Virtue. One of Paul's words for what to let into the mind, at home among the Greek philosophers too: the truly good, true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, of good report.
Your line: think on these things. True, honest, just, pure, lovely, of good report. Day six hundred sixty-seven, complete.

668.title: Content in all things (Philippians 4:10–23)
668.hook: I have learned to be content with little or plenty
668.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Philippians 4:11–13 in hard seasons and in seasons of plenty, and memorize the line about doing all things through Christ.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a list of whatever is lovely, and your line was think on these things.

A package arrives at a prison. Inside, maybe money, maybe food, maybe a warm cloak, sent a long way by friends who scraped it together. The man who opens it has been cold and hungry before, and he's been comfortable, too. Now he sits down to write a thank-you note. The last stretch of Philippians is partly that note, for a gift carried by Epaphroditus. But Paul, being Paul, can't just say thanks. He has to explain something he's learned, and it's as practical as anything in the letter.

He's glad for the gift, and almost in the same breath says he wasn't desperate for it. In the King James Bible: "for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." Learned. It didn't come naturally. Then: "I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need." Two things stand out. First, plenty is on the list. Contentment isn't only coping with too little. It's also not being owned by too much. Second, the word for instructed is unusual, a word used for being initiated into a secret, the way people were initiated into the mystery cults of the day. I've been let in on the secret, Paul says. And the secret is the next line, often quoted on its own: "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me." Read in its place, it isn't about winning a game or acing a test. It's about being hungry or full and staying steady either way. The word for content has a history too. Philosophers of Paul's day, the Stoics among them, prized it: being self-sufficient, needing nothing outside yourself. Paul shifts its center. Not self-sufficient. Sufficient in Christ. Then he thanks them warmly anyway, calls their gift "an odour of a sweet smell," and promises that God will supply all their need. The letter closes with greetings, even from people of Caesar's household. Philippians ends where it began: with joy, and with friends.
screen: then, large: `I HAVE LEARNED TO BE CONTENT.`

segments.voice: Look around you and name five things you already have, a chair, a window, a cup, a coat, your hands, without ranking them or wishing any were better; let each be enough for this minute. Then notice one want that keeps tugging at you, a thing to buy or to get, and let it sit there without obeying it. If you pray, you can give thanks for what's already here.
Contentment. Steadiness in plenty and in need. For Paul, it's learned, and it rests not on himself but on Christ who strengthens him.
Your line: I have learned contentment. Hungry or full, steady. That's Philippians, finished.

669.title: Count it all joy (James 1:1–8)
669.hook: trials produce patience; ask God for wisdom, who gives generously
669.howItsDone: Christians facing a decision sometimes pray the words of James 1:5, asking God for wisdom, and study groups often read the letter of James as a practical guide to everyday faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Philippians, and your line was I have learned contentment.

New letter, new voice. Paul wrote long, winding sentences. The letter of James is short and blunt, more like a book of proverbs than an argument. It's written to "the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad", believers living far from home. Tradition says the writer is James, the brother of Jesus, who led the church in Jerusalem. Churches hear that word brother differently. Protestants often take it plainly, a younger brother. Catholic tradition often speaks of a cousin or close relative, and Orthodox tradition of a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage. Either way, his very first instruction sounds upside down.

In the King James Bible: "My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations." Divers means various, and temptations here means trials, tests of every kind. Fall into, like a pit you didn't see. Count it all joy. Not feel it, count it: a decision about how you'll book the thing, not a mood. Why? "Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience." The word for trying means a test that proves what's genuine. And patience here is a strong word: endurance, the strength to keep going. Let it finish its work, James says, so you'll be whole, lacking nothing. And if you're in the middle of a trial and don't know what to do? "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him." Upbraideth not. In James's picture, God doesn't scold the one who asks. No sigh, no eye roll, no you should know this by now. Just generosity. One condition: ask in faith, without wavering, because the one who wavers "is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed." Such a person, he says, is double minded, literally double-souled. Not simply someone with questions. Someone pulled two ways at once, asking God for wisdom while planning not to listen.
screen: `COUNT IT JOY: A DECISION, NOT A MOOD.`
then, large: `LET HIM ASK OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're facing where you honestly don't know what to do, a decision at work, a relationship, a choice about money or health, and name it plainly. If you pray, ask God for wisdom about it in your own words; if you don't, sit with the question openly, as if an answer could come. Notice whether one part of you is asking while another part has already decided.
Endurance. James's strong word for patience: the strength trials build, so that letting it finish its work leaves you whole, lacking nothing.
Your line: ask for wisdom. The giver doesn't scold. Day six hundred sixty-nine, done.

staying calm and never feeling any pain
waiting quietly for someone else to act

670.title: Every good gift (James 1:9–18)
670.hook: every good gift comes from the Father of lights
670.howItsDone: James 1:17 is a favorite verse for thanksgiving services and harvest festivals, and many Christians recite it as a reminder that every good thing in their lives is a gift.

segments.voice: Yesterday, count it all joy, and your line was ask for wisdom.

Stand outside on a clear night and watch the sky for an hour. The moon moves. Stars rise in the east and sink in the west. Clouds slide across. Even the sun, by day, changes the length of every shadow from morning to evening. The lights in the sky are beautiful, but none of them stays put. Ancient people watched them closely and knew it. James is about to use that very picture. But first, something hard about where temptation comes from.

James starts with a reversal. Let the poor believer be proud of being lifted up, and the rich one glad to be brought low, because the rich fade like a flower in the field when the sun's heat rises. Then a blessing: "Blessed is the man that endureth temptation." And a warning, plain as a sign on a door: "Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God." Don't blame heaven. Temptation, James says, comes from inside, from our own desire, and it grows like a pregnancy: desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and sin, full grown, brings death. A hard image, and James means it to be. But he won't leave it there. "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning." In Genesis God makes the great lights, the sun and the moon and the stars, so James calls God their father, their maker. The lights move, they wane, their shadows turn, but the one who made them doesn't. God isn't moody. The good doesn't flicker on and off. And notice the direction. The bad grows up from below, out of desire. The good comes down from above, as gift. Then a last surprise: God, of his own will, "begat" us, gave us birth, by the word of truth. Two births in one passage. Desire gives birth to death. God gives birth to us.

Think back over the last day or two and find three good things you didn't earn: a kindness, a meal, a moment of beauty. Picture each one clearly and trace it back as far as you can: who gave it, who made it possible? If you pray, give thanks to the Father of lights for each; if you don't, simply receive them again, as gifts.
Variableness. The steadiness James gives to God, the Father of lights: with whom there is no variableness, neither shadow of turning, unlike the moving sky.
Your line: from the father of lights. No shadow of turning. Until tomorrow.

a wandering star that crosses the night sky

671.title: Quick to hear (James 1:19–27)
671.hook: swift to hear, slow to speak; pure religion visits orphans and widows
671.carry: swift to hear, slow to speak
671.howItsDone: Some churches name James 1:27 as the reason for their visiting ministries, food pantries and foster-care support.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Father of lights, with no shadow of turning, and your line was from the father of lights.

You're telling a friend something that matters. Halfway through, you can see it: they've stopped listening. Their eyes have that look. They're loading their reply. The second you take a breath, out it comes, about them. It's easy to end up on either side of that. James has three short rules for it. Then he holds up a mirror, and finally gives his own definition of what religion is for. It fits in one sentence.

In the King James Bible: "Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." Fast ears. Slow mouth. Slower temper. The order matters: if you're quick to hear, you're less likely to need the other two. Anger, James says, doesn't produce the kind of goodness God wants. Then he turns from listening to people to listening to God's word, and pushes one step further. "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves." Hearing is not the finish line. His picture: someone looks at their face in a mirror, sees it plainly, walks away, and "straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was." Spinach in your teeth. Hair sticking up. And you walk off and forget. That's hearing without doing. You saw it, and nothing changed. Then his definition: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world." Not a building. Not a feeling. Two things. Show up for the people with no one to protect them, and keep yourself clean. Care outward, integrity inward. The word for religion here means outward worship, the practice people could see. Put plainly: if you want to see someone's religion, watch where they go on a Tuesday afternoon.
screen: then, large: `SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.`

segments.voice: For a minute, just listen to the room: a fan, traffic, a bird, your own breathing, the farthest sound and the nearest. Notice how often your mind wants to comment, to name or judge what it hears, and let the comments go and keep listening. If you pray, you can ask for quick ears.
Doers. James's word for those who don't just hear but act: be doers of the word, not hearers only, or you deceive yourselves.
Your line: swift to hear, slow to speak. Doers, not hearers only. That's day six hundred seventy-one.

672.title: The gold ring (James 2:1–13)
672.hook: don't give the rich visitor the good seat and the poor one the floor
672.howItsDone: Some churches read James 2:1–9 when training greeters and welcome teams, as a check on who gets noticed at the door.

segments.voice: Yesterday, doers of the word, and your line was swift to hear, slow to speak.

Two people walk into a gathering at the same moment. One has a gold ring on his finger and fine clothes. The other is in shabby, dirty clothes. Watch where the eyes go. Watch who gets greeted first, who gets a chair, who gets a nod toward the back. Often nobody decides to do it. It just happens, in churches, restaurants, offices. James pictures it happening in the gatherings of early believers, so sharply you can almost hear the scrape of the chairs.

In the King James Bible: "For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment." The greeters say to the rich man: "Sit thou here in a good place"; and to the poor man: "Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool." On the floor, by someone's feet. James calls it judging with evil thoughts. A small detail: the Greek word for assembly here is synagogue, the ordinary word for a gathering. Some readers take it as a sign of how close these believers were to synagogue life. Then a question: "Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith?" The people sent to the floor are the ones God honors. Then he reaches for the royal law, the king's law, from Leviticus: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Favoritism breaks it. You can't love your neighbor as yourself while assigning seats by the shine of their jewelry. And a short, startling ending. Speak and act, he says, as people who will be judged by the law of liberty, because judgment will be without mercy to anyone who has shown no mercy. And then: "mercy rejoiceth against judgment." Modern versions say mercy triumphs over judgment. Picture a courtroom where mercy stands up and wins. This week has moved from Philippians into James: rejoice always, whatever is lovely, contentment, count it all joy, every good gift, quick to hear, and now the gold ring.

segments.voice: Picture the places you go in a normal week, a bus, a break room, a family table, and ask who usually gets the good seat, and who ends up quietly on the edge. Let one easy-to-overlook face come to mind, and picture making room for them: a chair pulled out, a question asked, your attention turned their way. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name.
Synagogue. The ordinary Greek word for a gathering, the word James uses for the believers' meeting, where the rich man gets the good seat and the poor man the floor.
Your line: mercy triumphs over judgment. The one who shows mercy is met by it. A week of letters, done.

fork.setup: you're greeting at the door. a man with a gold ring and a man in dirty clothes arrive together. there's one good seat left. what does James say happens?
options: the poor man gets it, because he's more in need.
the rich man gets it, and the poor man is sent to the floor.
neither gets it.
fork.reveal: "Sit thou here in a good place" to the rich, "sit here under my footstool" to the poor. James calls it judging with evil thoughts.

original.note: Greek: a gathering, an assembly. James uses it for the believers' meeting, the same word as synagogue.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about rude ushers.
what it means: favoritism breaks the royal law of love, and mercy wins over judgment.
what a scholar hears: 'your synagogue' in 2:2, and the royal law quoted from Leviticus 19:18, which some readers take as signs of the letter's Jewish roots.
recall: lights in the sky, as in Genesis

chat.says: Why does James make such a fuss about where people sit at a gathering?
options: Giving the rich the good seat breaks the royal law: love your neighbor as yourself.
He wanted the poor seated first and the rich sent to the back instead.
He thought the greeters were being rude to visitors who came in late.
chat.meaning: James calls favoritism judging with evil thoughts: it breaks the royal law, love your neighbor as yourself.

synagogue.meaning: Greek for a gathering; the word James uses for the assembly

royal law.meaning: James's name for love your neighbor as yourself

Leviticus.meaning: a book of the law of Moses, where the royal law is found
